utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to all of you as well. Mr. Mundis, I think the last thing you asked yesterday, how much time there would still be available. It would be 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Mundis: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday you told us that you do not recall precisely when you reviewed the transcript of the intercept or listened to the tape but that it was prior to reading the transcript of Major Indic's interview with the Prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the Prosecution disclosed the tape to the Defence in October 2001, and the Serbo-Croatian transcript in December 2001. Your report was filed in November 2002, so it would follow that you reviewed the transcript and listened to the tape sometime between December 2001 and November 2002. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only guess now. I can only try to read from the cards like a gypsy. But I said I really don't know when it was. I feel embarrassed having to tell you that I don't know when it was, but this is the fifth time I've told you that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you agree that if this tape and transcript are authentic that this material contained in the tape and transcript are significant to the issues in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could I ask this be done in the absence of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness please be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that sleeping on matters is beneficial sometimes, but apparently not always because yesterday the witness said that he couldn't check either the authenticity of the tape or of the transcript. He said that it wasn't part of his competence. He said that he couldn't check it. It's obvious that the witness is not in a position to comment on the authentic nature of an audiotape. We contested it ourselves. But how can such a witness confirm the authentic character of something which he knows by hearsay alone? And such a question, this type of question, is -- the purpose of this question is to embarrass the witness, to put him in a difficult situation, nothing else. It's obvious that the witness cannot comment on the authentic nature of the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please indicate where it is asked to comment on the authenticity of the tape. This is what you usually call a "question hypothetique," that is assuming something would be the case -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I agree that the expression itself implies if, if it's authentic. We agree. But nevertheless this witness has already clearly said there was nothing he could say about it. And this is the second part of my objection. If there is nothing he could say about it - I think he already said this yesterday - and we are going back to a subject that has already been addressed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness, as far as I understand, Mr. Mundis, is invited to tell us that if this would be an authentic copy, whether it would be of relevance, the witness has been -- or at least says that he reviewed the material. Therefore, I think we could ask questions about it. And if it finally turns out not to be authentic, then of course the Chamber will have to draw consequences. If it turns out to be authentic, then perhaps the consequences might be different. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I would like to add that the Defence also has the impression that when such questions are put in the way that the Prosecution put it, we are outside the framework determined by your Trial Chamber yesterday with regard to the type of questions to be put about such documents because we are addressing the substance of the matter; that is to say, the authenticity or the lack of such authenticity of this cassette. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers the question not to be -- the witness is not asked about whether these are authentic tapes. The witness is asked on whether, if authentic -- I would say the subject matter of the tape would be relevant. But, Mr. Mundis, you said relevant for the trial. Whereas we, yesterday have seen that there seems to be some confusion as to who decides what's relevant for the trial. But if you would limit that to the subject matter of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd please do so. Then, Madam Usher, can you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if this tape and transcript are authentic, what is contained in the tape and the transcript would be significant to the issues that you address in your report; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said before this Trial Chamber that I wrote my report on the basis of the operative documents of the sides. All the other documents had secondary importance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've listed a wide range of material that you relied on in producing your report. My question goes to the tape and transcript of what purports to be an intercept wherein General Mladic is issuing orders regarding shelling of certain areas of Sarajevo. If that tape and transcript are proven to be authentic, that would certainly be an important issue with respect to your report.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what my attitude towards tapes were. In my opinion, this material doesn't have the probative value of an operative document, so I couldn't assess its importance in that sense and rely on it. I reviewed this, just as I reviewed hundreds of documents. Occasionally I used this as an illustration when it corresponded to the data that I found in operative documents. But tapes or transcripts I didn't use as primary documents, but I did review them and tried to establish to what extent they corresponded to my findings -- to what I found out in operative documents. But with regard to this specific tape, you showed me a part of it, but I'm not familiar with the entire tape. I don't know what you're interested in exactly. I don't know about everything that you're interested in, so I cannot tell you whether this is important for me or not. I don't remember every transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've told us that you've reviewed the tape and the transcript of the -- what appears to be an intercept of General Mladic. In the intercept, it appears that he is ordering shelling of the city of Sarajevo. You've told us that you primarily looked at operative documents. Are you telling us that if we have an intercept of an oral order by the commander of the VRS that that would not be of significance in preparing your report? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For my report that would have had importance if it concerned the period during which General Galic was the commander. If this was an order issued to General Galic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you. You've mentioned the period during which General Galic was the commander. You have read the indictment that the Prosecution prepared against General Galic and you've read the pre-trial brief which the Prosecution filed. Is it not clear from those two documents that the Prosecution has alleged that General Galic in effect assumed command whereby a pre-existing campaign was in existence? Is that not clear from the documents from the Prosecution which you have read?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the Prosecution's claim, but the findings contradict that claim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the issue is whether or not you would have found the contents of the tape and transcript significant for purposes of your report.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not enough just to hear what is said on a tape. It's necessary to know who said what, when, to whom, in what period of time. It's necessary to know the context. It's necessary to know what was happening in Sarajevo at that time. These are facts on the basis of which this answer should be answered. It's not possible to take this out of context and then comment on this because then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Then what I -- the information I provide you with would not be reliable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, witness: This intercept is not referred to anywhere in your report, is it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it is referred to in your report or yes, it is not referred to in your report? Is it referred to in the report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question was formed as a claim. In your report -- this intercept isn't mentioned in your report; is that correct? And I said yes, it's not mentioned in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, it would seem that in light of your previous answer with respect to placing the intercept in context and to know what was happening that the proper place to do that would have been in your report.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wouldn't. If I were to write the report now after having spoken to you about this matter, I still wouldn't include it in the report because this is something that didn't occur during the term of office of General Galic and that is a period during which war was raging in Sarajevo and all JNA features had been attacked and all Serbian settlements had been fiercely attacked by the Muslim forces. And to take this out of context and not analyse everything else would be imprecise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, there is a wide wealth of material in your report dealing with issues before the indictment period. Why was this tape and transcript not dealt with in a similar manner, in light of the fact that you have discussed at great length a series of events that occurred before General Galic assumed command?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discussed the events before General Galic assumed command to show how the forces ended up in the Sarajevo theatre. I wanted to demonstrate the situation to the Trial Chamber, to show that there was a war in Sarajevo and that it wasn't a matter of some wild Serbs having descended from the hills, who started terrorising the civilians. I wanted to show that there was a war, that they engaged in a conflict, and that that conflict had certain consequences. That was the purpose of my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think that you can gain a picture of this from my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there, witness. Does it not seem from the transcript or tape of this intercept that what General Mladic was ordering goes to the very issue of terrorising the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I'd ask that it be done in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'm assuming that we are still discussing matters hypothetically. If we assume that this transcript is something real and assuming that the voice we hear is that of General Galic and assuming that there is a certain Vukanovic, assuming all of this, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- If we assume all this and if we assume that it isn't fabricated, in this attempt we are trying to return to the substance, that is to say, the general quite clearly said that everything depends on the context. Everything depends on the context, and he quite clearly said that he couldn't answer if he's not aware of the context. If he is told that if we don't know in relation to what this order was issued, perhaps there was an ongoing operation, perhaps the barracks were blocked, we know that they were in the month of May - this is one of possible questions - but we can't put to question to him as such if he is not provided with all the contextual elements. This is too microscopic view of the problem and it is then blown up to present a false image of the situation on the ground, of the reality. So this is a distorted form, a distorted version of what should have been done, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, the Prosecution is attempting to adduce this information because it goes to the methodology that this expert used in preparing his report. At no time have we suggested that this witness could authenticate anything, nor have we -- I'm not quite sure what the objection is with respect to microscopic view of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the objection mainly is that where the witness has testified that he could not give any comment on the matter unless he would know more details. It is not possible to characterise the subject matter of the conversation without knowing more details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from the objection, Mr. Mundis, the Chamber invites you to move on. The issue has been sufficiently dealt with, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, can you please escort the witness into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm now going to return to the issue of the interviews that you personally conducted. You told us on page 6 of your report that you interviewed a number -- a series of outstanding superior officers of the SRK and direct participants in the war at Sarajevo battlefield, and you also spoke with seven UNPROFOR and UN military observers. If you tally up the numbers presented on page 6, it would appear that you interviewed 34 individuals. We have your notes from 11 of those interviews, and you told us that you didn't take notes with respect to the other individuals; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, these 34 individuals that you interviewed, how were those -- how was the initial contact with those 34 individuals established? Did you prepare a list of 34 individuals that you wanted to interview? Did the Defence legal team arrange that? How did that come to pass that you interviewed these 34 individuals?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conceptualised my methodology of work. Then of course I drafted my own plan of work. Under number 1 came the operative information from the parties. In the second place I put -- I can't explain it to you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. otherwise, except by telling you the sequence in which I proceeded. If you want me to answer, I'll answer. If you don't want me to answer, you can reply yourself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the question is: How were these 34 individuals selected and how did you make the initial contact with these individuals?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The persons were chosen by me, and I contacted them through the Defence team. Specifically, I agreed my study trips with Mrs. Pilipovic and I always travelled with her. She had the authority to enable me to speak to these people. Some of these people were in Belgrade, and I occasionally saw them in Belgrade, not only on the site. As far as UNPROFOR members are concerned, those were members of the Russian Battalion and the members of the UNMO from Moscow. I went on one occasion with Mrs. Pilipovic to Moscow and talked to them. And I was primarily interested in the Monitoring Mission, how they gathered information, how they drafted their reports, how they sent them. This part was not quite clear to me, so I wanted to get first-hand information. I was particularly interested in this part, in learning about this part from Mr. Indic. And since this contained very little of that kind of information, I was not particularly interested in that transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's -- you've classified these individuals according to their positions. Let's start with the two corps commanders. You indicate that you interviewed two corps commanders. It would appear from your notes that one of those was General Djurdjevac, the commander of the JNA 4th Corps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you interview Dragomir Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when you interviewed Dragomir Milosevic? Where did that interview take place?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I'd ask that it be done in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, on the other hand, we are not going to -- I think you have these little houses where the people turn in and out according to whether the weather is better or worse. We're not going to do this. Could you say in one word - so not argument - but is it relevance? Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Yes, Your Honour. It's a question that's purely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking -- is it about relevance that you're -- I mean, what is very often done is that you just indicate in what field the objection should be sought. If there would be needed further argument, then of course we have to ask the witness to leave the courtroom. But sometimes one word is enough. Is it relevance or is it ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I said, Your Honour, relevance to the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, it goes to methodology and perhaps credibility. I can't elaborate more upon that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought I said in French immediately "objection, relevance," but that's what I said in French from the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it is clear now, so there's no need to reiterate the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this very moment the relevance is not clear. But if you want to come back to that specific question, we'll perhaps do it after the break and then you can explain. But at this moment, please proceed with another question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you interview any other corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To be quite clear, Mr. Mundis, it was about the place of the interview that our ruling was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to Dragomir Milosevic, when did you interview him?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Same. And at this stage, Mr. President, I would like to say something in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll ask the witness to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd ask that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd ask that this be done in private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then turn into private session, unless -- but Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if the matter you would like to raise should not be done in private session, then we'll first give an opportunity to the Prosecution to explain the -- what in their view the relevance of the question is, and then we could return in open session and you can make observations as needed. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. President, that this should be done in public session. I don't know what the method is that's used. Maybe we go into private session and then we go back into public session. I am at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll first turn into private session. It seemed that we were, but now it's not on our screen any more. So -- yes, we are in private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, there was an issue you'd like to raise in open session. You told us before. Or was this the matter you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No -- yes, Mr. President. I was trying to say that these questions should be asked in public session. You decided otherwise, but we are at your service. We thought that this should be settled in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could the witness be brought into the courtroom again. Mr. Mundis, oh, you're just waiting for the witness to re-enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us again on page 6 that you interviewed two chiefs of staff of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. What were the names of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Dragan Marcetic and Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused, witness. You -- in response to a question about corps commanders, you gave us the name Dragomir Milosevic. It's true he was previously chief of staff of the SRK. Who did you include in the category of the two corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain one thing, please. I spoke to Mr. Milosevic, both as corps commander, as chief of staff of the corps, and as commander of the 216th, that is, the 1st Romanija Brigade. So you will find him in three places in my interviews. The chief of staff position was occupied by both Dragan Marcetic and Milosevic, and I talked to both of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you list the interviews by their functional titles in your report, some of these individuals would have counted more than once. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made -- in fact, if I had made a list of persons in an attachment, I would have written that I have spoken to Milosevic in his three capacities, with Sajlovic in two of his capacities, but I didn't think that was necessary and I didn't do it. It is insignificant. I can explain this here if you want to take my word for it. If not, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have some time constraints, witness. Let me ask you about the seven brigade commanders that you've indicated you interviewed. Who were those brigade commanders and which brigades did they command?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's begin with the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. The person is Stojanovic. Then going eastward, according to the operative disposition, the commander of the 1st Romanija Brigade was Lizdek; commander of the same brigade, Milosevic; and commander of the 216th Brigade from Han Pijesak, which came to the Sarajevo theatre in May, commander was Milosevic, and I spoke to him about this aspect of the theatre of war. The commander of the Kosevo Brigade was Mr. Krajisnik. The commander of the Ilijas Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wonder if I can say this here. If by mentioning certain names we are not falling into the same trap as before. I know that the witness himself is doing it, but we should be cautious about this. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed. But it's inappropriate to deal with the matter in the presence of the witness, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you were interrupted, you were about to give us the name of the commander of the Ilijas Brigade that you interviewed in preparing your report. Can you please continue.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A young man by the name of Savic. I think Savic is his name. The commander of the Ilidza Brigade, Radojcic, and Sehovac, who was commander of the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also indicate that you interviewed two chiefs of brigade staff. Can you please tell us who these two individuals were and of which brigades they served as chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of staff of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade was Sajlovic, and before that he used to be a commander of one mechanised battalion, whereas commander of the Ilijas Brigade used to be chief of staff of that brigade previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say the commander of the Ilijas Brigade, would that again be the individual with the name Savic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us also that you interviewed two security officers. Who were those two individuals?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Lugonja and Bukva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next category is three battalion commanders. Who were those three individuals and which battalions did they command, please?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was the commander of the battalion at Hresa. I don't know his name. One was the commander of the battalion at Grbavica. And the third was the commander of the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade at Vojkovici. I must tell you that I honestly don't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then told us that you interviewed some, as you characterised it, fighters. And you mentioned four fighters from Grbavica. Who were these individuals that you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the names. I can't remember the names, to tell you the truth. I can't remember the names of the soldiers because I spoke to them very briefly. I just wanted to feel what the atmosphere was like, to see how they felt when the front was 200 metres away or even closer. That's the atmosphere that interested me from the psychological point of view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't remember them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that you interviewed three fighters from Nedzarici. What were their names?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were fighters at the front line. They used nicknames, you know. They're still afraid of being identified on the basis of their names because the consequences of the war are still present there and they're very reluctant to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated that you interviewed two fighters from Dobrinja. Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember the names of the fighters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us earlier in setting up the interviews that you prepared the list of individuals that you wanted to speak with. Does that include these nine fighters from Grbavica, Nedzarici, and Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that I made a list of soldiers, but I decided on the sort of people I wanted to speak to. But I didn't make a list because that didn't depend on me, whether we found these people didn't depend on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you prepared a list of the types of people you wanted to speak with, and then the Defence legal team prepared the list of people for you to speak to and made arrangements for you to speak to them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What's the problem, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem. I want to draw your attention to it now. Page 23, line 6 and 7. It seems that the English booth did not fully reproduce what the witness said, or that the French booth added something, because we don't have the same thing in both transcripts. I know that the French booth mentioned discussions with Mrs. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have to check whether the translation of your words is complete and correct, General. In the English translation, your answer to a question reads: "No, I didn't say that I made a list of soldiers, but I decided on the sort of people I wanted to speak to. But I didn't make a list because that didn't depend on me, whether we found these people didn't depend on me." Is there anything extra you said which is -- does not appear in this translation of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you then now, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what appears in the French translation which does not appear --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I asked for this to be confirmed because I'm only using one set of headphones today, which is not my custom. Mrs. Pilipovic tells me that she heard that the general said that it also depended -- General Radinovic said that this depended also on interviews with Mrs. Pilipovic, because she was the person who could guide her in relation to these contacts. This was translated into French, but apparently it wasn't translated by the English booth. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it correct that you said that it depended on your -- we could check it in the original, but if you could confirm that you said that it depended on your interviews with Ms. Pilipovic. If you said this, please confirm it. If you didn't say it, then it's -- one of the two booths translated different from the other, and we could check the original, but if you could help us out, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned Mrs. Pilipovic in this context, in the following context: I didn't personally contact these people, but it was through Mrs. Pilipovic, or rather, her team. I don't know whether she arranged for this or someone from her team, but for me the only thing that was important was that I should tell her about what and with whom I wanted to speak, and that is why I mentioned Mrs. Pilipovic in my answer, so all contacts with the people that I spoke to went through Mrs. Pilipovic, or rather, her office, her team, her associates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Mr. Mundis, you were interrupted where you were about to ask a question. Could you please repeat the question, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the question was: You prepared a list of the types of people you wanted to speak with and then the Defence legal team prepared the list of people for you to speak with and made arrangements for you to speak with them. You've --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you haven't understood me correctly. The Defence didn't make a list. I told the Defence that I wanted to speak to commanders -- to brigade commanders, and then I said that I would like to -- when going to certain places, I said that I would like to speak to certain people in those places and I would like contact with certain people in certain places so that we could talk about certain issues that I was interested in. That's how we proceeded. When we went to Sarajevo, I said that I would like to speak to people in Sarajevo on that day, people who were in the SRK, and I had contact with a lot of people in Belgrade and this was through Mrs. Pilipovic, apart from the fact that we used her offices for discussions. Well, I didn't need that kind of intervention. But since she was my host, we did all of these things through her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, may I invite you to conclude within a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us you interviewed seven UNPROFOR or other UN personnel. Do you remember the names of any of these United Nations personnel?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the commander of the UNPROFOR Russian Battalion, Vorobev, he was also a witness as far as I know here, and I followed that testimony live. I don't remember the other names because I didn't obtain anything particular in the course of speaking to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name was Vorobev.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, other than the names that you've given us this morning and of course Mrs. Galic, that you told us yesterday, did you interview anyone else other than the people you mentioned this morning and Mrs. Galic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in official communications, but in professional terms, yes, perhaps I did, but I can't really remember. But officially, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on page 64 of the English translation of your report, footnote 72, there's a reference to a statement of Kojovic given to the Defence. Did you interview anyone by the name of Kojovic and do you know who that person is?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Koljevic, it's Kojovic, Kojovic, the pre-war minister for culture and information in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the director of Sarajevo Television. On a study trip to Banja Luka, I had the pleasure of having dinner with him, and it was a totally informal conversation. It had nothing to do with the report, but I read his statement, and in particular I read his book called "The Bloody Sarajevo Shirt," and it talks about the war in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I have just a couple of remaining questions. Page 167, footnote 252 of your report you also make reference to information of General Zdravko Tolimir, deputy commander of VRS main staff for intelligence, security affairs. Did you interview General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We have a certain number of questions, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we'll first of all start with what you said today and then we will examine what you said yesterday in relation to questions put to you by the Prosecution. First of all, good day. I'd like to go back to the numerous questions put to you about the well-known document which is apparently a transcript of a tape on which there is a Serbian general and another Serbian officer, and it apparently concerns the shelling of Sarajevo. My first question is a methodological one: What do you do when you have a document the sources of which have not been identified, not in a sufficiently credible or serious way, a document which doesn't have a date of any kind or any information that would make it possible to establish a date for such a document? And could you answer this question purely in methodological terms.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as the methodology is concerned, this isn't a document that I could accept as a relevant one for my analysis. But as far as the facts contained in that document, this could be a reason for checking in operative documents, checking this in operative documents, checking in sources that I said were relevant. Perhaps something could be found in such operative documents. This could be a reason for further investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. To make sure that we have understood you correctly, the documents that you saw or attached to your expert report and the documents on which you based your report, did you verify the dates, the fact that they had dates, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. General, let's imagine that the date of the 12th of May, 1992 was a date that one had to remember. And as I said, let's imagine this. You spoke about the relation to context, the importance of context. Could you tell us what you meant to say when you were interrupted by the Prosecution. What was happening in Sarajevo around the 12th of May, 1992? Could you briefly give us certain elements, certain -- could you tell us about certain event, certain facts that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-May -- well, there was almost no area in Sarajevo where the war wasn't raging. That was a time which more or less overlapped with an operation carried out by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. It still hadn't become the official Army of BH. It was called the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the so-called Pofalicki battle, the bottle for Pofalici, as the commander of the Territorial Defence, Hasan Efendic says in his book. They still celebrate this as a great victory, but in fact it was an attack on the Serbian settlement of Pofalici, and over 200 people, mostly civilians, were killed on that occasion. That was the time when Grbavica was attacked frontally. It was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. Before that there was a mass attack on Ilidza. Nedzarici was constantly under fire. There was an attack on Rajlovac towards the end of May. Efendic also writes about this in his book. Vogosca was also attacked and many people were killed on that occasion. That was a period during which the war was extremely intense. It was the most intense period of fighting in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, during this period of time, mid-May - we're talking about this period in relation to this document - in inverted commas, these attack, these military operations you have mentioned, did they include mounting operations, logistics -- on the level of logistics, troops, et cetera, in the centre of Sarajevo, according to your expertise as a professional member of the military?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. Beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, absolutely not. We wanted to discuss this document at length. The general said it would be necessary to place it in its proper context. I'm just asking whether the context makes it necessary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the purpose of taking that witness to that document related to the methodology and credibility of the witness with respect to a statement he had made. We certainly did not in our view open up the door to a lengthy discussion on the contents of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I sat down as a matter of courtesy, but I think that everyone saw that I hadn't concluded. But I should be allowed to finish. I have nothing against genies out of bottles, but I should be allowed to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's try to minimise the theatrical part of the debate in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly, Mr. President. To return to more specific matters, was this witness aware in technical terms of the fact that it was necessary to group people in the centre of the city or not. This is the expert who is supposed to tell us whether such attacks took place on the line because one snapped one's fingers or were there serious preparations. This is an expert. He can tell us about this. And if we are told that this is not within the sphere of his competence, this is barely acceptable. It's almost theatrical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I earlier asked you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, not always to echo my comments on what the parties do. Would you please refrain from that. To a limited extent you'll be allowed to ask the witness questions about the context. To a limited extent because the witness has testified that he could not answer the question of the relevance of the audiotape without looking in more detail to the context. That means that the context to the extent of importance for the witness not being able to answer the question is relevant and arises from cross-examination. The context as a, well, part of the conflict of Sarajevo in general terms does not arise from cross-examination. So one or two questions in this respect so that the witness can explain himself, I'll allow it, and then please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Gladly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One question, witness: Mounting operations, what can you tell us about the principle -- about how such operations were mounted in principle? And I'm not asking about what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was a period of time during which the inner part of the city, the part of the city mentioned on the tape, operations were mounted from that part of the city in the direction of the Army of Republika Srpska, or the fronts that it held, and also towards Serbian settlements such as Grbavica, Velesici, Nedzarici, Ilidza, Vogosca, et cetera. And the fact that from the very centre of the town, that the army headed out from there and that it was used for basing the army there, because of that it was a legitimate target. So what you could hear on the tape could be legitimate, in spite of the fact that it seems terrible. I'm just discussing this from the point of view of military doctrine. If you have an active enemy, it's quite legitimate to counter attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we will now move to certain responses that you provided to questions put to you by the Prosecution yesterday. I'm referring to pages yesterday. On page 5 of the transcript yesterday you spoke about anti-sniper units, but you didn't finish what you were saying. I would appreciate it if you could add something and tell us why there were such anti-sniper units.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, anti-sniper units existed because combat with snipers is the most difficult part of combat. It's the most efficient way -- the most efficient way to eliminate a sniper is to use a sniper, provided that you detect the sniper and provided that the position from which fire is being opened can be reached, is accessible. UNPROFOR insisted and the Serbian side too, they insisted on reaching an anti-sniper agreement and on forming units which would deal with snipers. As far as I know, UNPROFOR also had an anti-sniper unit and on several occasions it eliminated snipers on the Muslim side in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You provided certain answers yesterday on page 12 and the pages that followed. You mentioned documents that you were able to consult, and you mentioned the documents you had access to. You mentioned the military archives, and my question is as follows: The BH army archives, were they made accessible to you and were you able to gain access to those documents?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The archives of the BH army were not open to me, because that's in another state. I'm not a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina and I could not gain access to the archives, but I did examine documents from that side on the basis of the documents that the Prosecution provided to the Defence, and there were quite a lot of documents. Naturally, the ones that I mentioned were missing and that had to do with the civil part of command, so the political strategy and military strategy in the context of political strategy cannot be observed. I think that this is a weakness perhaps in my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you think that the BH archives exist somewhere according to your information? Do you know how they are treated today? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think they do exist, because given the documents that I examined here - because as you know, I've been here on two occasions to examine documents that the Prosecution provided to the Defence, documents which have to do with the documents of the BH army 1st Corps - that consisted of many documents and these documents were very well ordered, and I was able to come to the conclusion that these archives had been very well organised and put in good order, and I hope that there will be a time when these archives will be accessible and it will be a great satisfaction to be able to use what these archives -- the documents that these archives have. I mean, it will be a great satisfaction for investigative purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 18, General, you said that there were no sniper units. I'd like you to provide us with more information and to tell us on what kind of information you -- on the basis of what kind of information you provided such a claim.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my claim is based on operative documents, above all. Not in a single document of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps did I come across indications that there were special sniper units. Not a single document issued by the commander of the corps, his deputy acting as commander, not a single document mentions a separate sniper unit under the command of the corps commander. Likewise, I personally didn't come across any indications according to which there were special units in brigades under the command of brigade commanders. I'm referring to sniper units. The only indication of a special sniper unit in the brigades of the SRK was found in a document provided by the Prosecution, and it has to do with a sniper section as part of the 1st Ilijas Light Infantry Brigade. And this is something that I heard in the course of the testimony of the Prosecution expert, Mr. Philipps. I examined this document, and I must admit that it raised certain doubts -- I have certain doubts as to its authenticity, but I'm not going to comment on that because this is not my field. This document doesn't have a stamp. So the form of the document is not right. But as this is not my sphere of competence, I'm not going to tell you what my reservations are. But I didn't find any confirmation in any other document that might show that there were sniper units within the SRK. I didn't come across such information in documents, and not a single brigade commander with whom I spoke confirmed that he had a sniper unit. All of them told me that they had snipers. Of course they had snipers in sections, but far fewer than you might expect in terms of the establishment. And they did not have sniper units that they would have used as a manoeuvre force, sniper units they would have issued orders to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, a few questions about sniper units. Did you ask commanders direct questions about the existence of sniper units in brigades?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when they replied, how did you perceive this response? Was it doubtful? Was it timid? Was it quite clear? Was it a response that you thought was truthful?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these answers corresponded fully to my previous view of this situation, my previous knowledge of the establishment of the brigades of the SRK. I know what the formations looked like. When you form an army, you have so-called formation books, and in the formation books they don't mention sniper units as special units within brigades, and this only confirmed what I knew. If I had found something that contradicted this in the documents, I would have taken this into account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we'll continue this subject after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I think it's time to have a break now, Mr. President. Perhaps we should have a break now, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you indicate how much time you would approximately need.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a dozen questions or so. I'm going to try to control the witness's answers to make sure that they are a little shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 12 questions, 20 minutes would be fair, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to economise, both in your own words and in the words of the witness, and we'll see where it ends. But certainly not much longer than 20 minutes. Then we'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I see that you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. President, in view of the answers given by the current witness during the morning session, I have an application to make. I'd seek to make it in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While waiting and to economise time, the document dated the 12th of June, 1993, which is the one that we examined yesterday, I think the Defence number is D259, it could be placed on the ELMO. And I have the same request to make with regard to a document the number of which is D64 [as interpreted]. That is to save time, Mr. President. It hasn't been correctly entered into the transcript because we have 264.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: 264, please. That's the number I gave. Do you have some difficulties -- yes, that's all right now. Thank you. [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know if Madam Registrar has found the documents, but I could show them to her so that we are sure that we have these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that we start with document number 259.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it please be put on the ELMO so that we are certain that there's no mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, to your right you have a document. Is this document dated the 12th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you read out the second paragraph, I think. Do you remember that; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you briefly read out the following paragraph, that is to say, paragraph 3 that starts with the word "upozoravam," "I warn." And the fourth paragraph too, could you do that very quickly.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. It's beyond the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The objection is denied. The -- you limited your questions during cross-examination to one line of this document, and the context -- the Defence should be in a position to create the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, could you read these two paragraphs very rapidly, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I hereby warn unit commanders that criminal proceedings shall be instituted against irresponsible and wilful officers. All officers and soldiers should be told, should be explained what the consequences of irresponsible and wilful behaviour will be."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Saving ammunition is the primary task. We have exhausted supply sources. It is not possible to obtain ammunition."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Explain to soldiers and officers that they should only open fire when ordered to do so and authorised to do so by their officers and they should only open fire on visible targets and when this is essential. Soldiers and officers who disobey and are irresponsible should be held responsible and they should be reported so that criminal proceedings are instituted against them."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, according to your experience of military documents, does this document have a stamp, et cetera, a signature? Does it appear to you to be an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The authenticity does not arise from cross-examination, I would take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. And the Prosecution again would like to articulate an objection to this line of questioning on the grounds that the Defence had ample opportunity to go through these documents in their direct examination, they chose not to. These are Defence exhibits, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, Mr. Mundis. On the other hand, these documents have been introduced in a rather general way, and in the time restraints, that is understandable. Nonetheless, the Prosecution cross-examination sought to have one single line read out of this document, and under these circumstances the Defence is allowed to then have a couple of more lines read out as well. But it would give rise to me for one question for you, specifically in view of the last line you read, General Radinovic. Did you come across any reports or subsequent criminal charges in respect of such incidents? And I'm referring to the last line, where it says that if you violate this order, then soldiers and officers could be prosecuted for that. Did you come across any such prosecutions or reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't come across any documents on criminal prosecutions, but I did come across documents in which requests were made to investigate cases and to establish the responsibility of the persons concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you come across any reports as a consequence of such investigations ordered? I mean, ordering an investigation usually results in a report of the investigator. Did you come across any report of such investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I came across such reports, and I referred to those reports in my report, reports in which commanders respond to the requests from their superior commands, from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, with regard to certain incidents. I mentioned them in my report. In most of those reports the questions are answered as to whether they're responsible for opening fire and why fire was opened. On the whole, it is explicitly stated that they were either responding to fire or that they didn't take action from their positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So -- yes, I do understand. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the question I'm going to put to you has to do with document 264. I'm going to ask you whether you remember it. It mentions an order from the army which says that measures should be taken to spare civilians on the other side who remain in Serbian territory. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. Beyond the scope. This document was not put to the witness during the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was indirectly, Mr. President. First of all, by us and then there was a question of a general nature put to the witness by the Prosecution. They asked whether he had found the document showing -- establishing the conclusions he reached. The Prosecution asked such questions. They wanted to know which documents he was basing himself in order to reach his conclusions, and my question is to see what the intention was and to see whether certain documents concern this matter. This is with regard to the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. It does not sufficiently arise out of cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll forget that document and we'll refer to document 259.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do such orders on the basis of your experience conform to what one should do? I'm talking about document 259. It's still on the screen. Do such orders, in your opinion, conform to what a commander should do if and when such problems arise? And I'm referring to the Geneva Conventions. I'm making a direct reference to the Geneva Conventions or to other conventions.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It seems quite appropriate to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we assume that the signatory of this letter, who is, I think -- the name isn't important, but he's a colonel.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Marcetic, the deputy commander of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom did he probably receive these orders? From which level did he receive these orders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, this is really -- I just told you to what extent and for what reasons it was allowed that other parts would be read, but you're now entering a totally new area that's -- although, you do it on the basis of this document, but that goes beyond what the Chamber allowed you to do, apart from that it's also speculation. So would you please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Gladly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to go back to the issue of snipers. You were asked a certain number of questions about snipers, rifles, your personal notes that you showed on the screen, et cetera. My question is: Did you often see or did you rarely see orders, specific orders coming from the corps or from the SRK that concerned opening fire on the line? And I mean -- I'm referring to infantry weapons in particular.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have come across documents governing the opening of fire. Restrictions related to the use of opening -- or opening of mortar fire or calibres upward of 7.6 millimetres. In documents there is no mention of imposed restrictions because fire is opened when the situation requires it. That is, when there is fire from the opposite side, fire is returned from the contact line, the separation line. So restrictions are imposed exclusively during truces or cease-fires, when appropriate agreements exist, and it is the obligation of immediately superior officers on the front line to regulate the return of fire when there is fire from the opposite side. That is the obligation of officers on the spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to show this witness a document that was examined at length yesterday. It was also produced as D10, but this document includes five points, P10413.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or P3413, correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document that was shown yesterday to this witness exists, therefore, in several versions, but we want to take the one we saw yesterday and to save time, to save time I would like to ask this witness from page 3. I would like him to read from page 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have this document? I think so. So from page 3 -- sorry, page 4. Would the witness kindly read item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has this text been placed before the witness?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Item 2 of the summary of the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean "At the end of the meeting Colonel Galic proposed the following conclusions"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now item 2.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To implement the conclusions from the Banja Luka meeting, which conclusions should be delivered to unit commands and municipalities."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now bullet 2, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To preserve the current positions and to defend them without waging war."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, isn't there a contradiction in terms between the requirement to defend without waging war and what we heard yesterday, namely that the town should be razed to the ground?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we would like to present 1926 now, and we would like to witness to read it.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To your question, of course. These two things are diametrically opposite. If you defend your positions peacefully, then you can't at the same time raze the town to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution objects to this document being shown to the witness, again on the grounds that it could have been put to him in direct, it doesn't arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I don't know whether this is a matter that should be discussed in the presence of the witness, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be better for the witness to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, I'll ask you to escort the witness out of the courtroom. I'm sorry for you, General Radinovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is something I have to do more often than anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. To be quite honest, it is not quite true. We ourselves spent some time on it. And thank you for this additional hour. We selected our questions carefully. As for the Prosecution, they decided themselves to intervene and to ask questions about the alleged fifth objective of the Serb side. We have here a document which is not a transcript a posteriori, which is a summary of the conclusions of the meeting. It is dated not the 14th but the 12th from that notorious meeting. And now considering what is item 5 here, we see clearly that the necessity to raze to the ground the city of Sarajevo is not in question here. We have opposite evidence, evidence to the contrary, namely that Sarajevo was a very important place in the strategic game that was going on. But we would like to show this witness other documents. And if we didn't do it before, it's because that we didn't know that the Prosecution was going to raise this issue. Of course we cannot know in advance everything that may be raised here as an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I understand the questions of the Prosecution well that it was not -- whether it was true or not what item 5 said, but whether the expert considered it worth mentioning it, since true or not it is at least a document which casts a different light -- true or not but casts a different light, compared to other documents, on the events and that it was not mainly the issue of exploring whether it was true or not? The expert, when asked about whether he found it useful to mention it didn't say, "No, I did not use that because it is contradicted by another document I reviewed," but -- so would you please give us the questions you would like to put to that witness -- to the expert witness so that we can consider whether this would arise from cross-examination or deals with another subject. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will take the liberty of specifying certain things, in fact adding to what you said. I have in mind the context because two types of questions were asked of this

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: item 5; and the second that links up with the first is to read out to this witness that General Galic, who was colonel at the time, asked that these five points from the other meeting be accepted, be adopted. Thus the question was formulated in such a way as to infer the possibility that General Galic asked the participants to adopt something which amounted to the strategy of destroying Sarajevo. That is how the questions from the Prosecution were formulated. What we want to show is that the minutes from this notorious meeting do not mention anywhere the destruction of Sarajevo in item 5. There is mention of division but not the intention to raze Sarajevo to the ground. It is a basic distinction that we would like to have the opportunity of making.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the issue of what the facts are and whether the expert should have explained on the basis of this document that it was not correct what the other document says is -- there's a very thin line between dealing with the facts and dealing with the methodology used by the expert witness. And since in my consultations with the other Judges I found that one of the Judges had already in mind to ask some questions about it, I would prefer that these questions first be put to the expert witness. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is going -- I don't know for sure that I have followed correctly. Who is going to ask questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I've got your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Nieto-Navia. Yes. General Radinovic, you've just been presented with a document and one of the Judges, Judge Nieto-Navia, has one or more questions to you in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I am taking advantage of the fact that you have the document there. Yesterday a document was shown to you which supposedly contains the report on a meeting of military commanders and the presidents of municipalities. That document mentions a meeting in Banja Luka where strategic goals were formulated. My first question is: Is that session in Banja Luka the same one that you mentioned in page 50 - I am talking of the English version of your report - item 102 under number "1"? Do you have your report there? Please look at number 102.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: There you say that "such allegations are not true for several reasons: 1." And you mention a session of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska in Banja Luka. So my question is whether the mention made in the second report, the one that was shown to you yesterday, page 3, according to which some strategic goals were formulated in Banja Luka is the same meeting that you are referring to here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mean the session of the 12th of May, 1992, which is the sixteenth session of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then yes. But I was also shown yesterday a document related to the meeting in Mrkonjic Grad, and I'm not sure, maybe you mean that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... The document that we saw yesterday. I don't have an exhibit number, but it's the one related to a meeting of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 259, I believe, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: 259. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3413.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: This one, yes. These go to page 3. I think that it is the same in both versions. The second full paragraph mentions the strategic goals formulated at a meeting in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A crucial difference is between the formulation of objective 5 in this document compared to the objective --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: No, no, no. My question is: When you make a reference to the meeting in Banja Luka in your report --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: -- Is it the same meeting referred to in that document? Do you think so? When we are talking about strategic goals formulated in Banja Luka, is it the same meeting you are referring to in your report in the part that we have looked at a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my report I referred to the minutes of the session of the Assembly of Republika Srpska, that is, in item 102 of my report. On the second page of this paragraph 102 I mentioned this document, showing how the objective adopted at the Assembly of Republika Srpska was misrepresented in this document. The objective was rephrased in a very important manner and therefore this document is absolutely useless for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: If I understand you well, when you mentioned here the meeting in Banja Luka and the strategic goals of that meeting, you are referring to this document, to the one that you have there. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not this one. Not this document. The minutes from the session of the assembly, as published in the Serbian gazette, in an official document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Let me say something. We have a meeting of the assembly that was held on the 14th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not the 14th. The 12th of May, 1992 is the date when the assembly session was held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: That's correct. Then we have another document dated the 14th May 1992, which is supposed to be a meeting between the presidents of municipalities. That's the one that you have there. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: In that second meeting, a reference is made to the strategic goals formulated at the meeting in Banja Luka. That reference is made to the document of 12th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Okay. Now we have -- the second issue is that in number 5 of the second document, the one of the 14th of May, it says that it was said that Sarajevo must be either divided or razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what's written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Then the question is whether that statement was in fact one of the strategic goals formulated in Banja Luka on the 12th of May. If you want, you can have a look on the minutes of the session held on 12th May. I don't know which is the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 8. It's on page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: In page 14 of the English version, mention is made to the fifth strategic goal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.
