utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: That paragraph, please have a look on that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it before me. Shall I read?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You have it before you. Can it be summarised as it was summarised at the meeting of the 14th May, that is, it was said that Sarajevo must be either divided or razed to the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in this paragraph. In this paragraph it says that the fifth strategic objective is to divide the city of Sarajevo into the Muslim and Serbian parts and to establish efficient governments in each of these parts of town with elements of constituent states. That's what's written in the original minutes of the original meeting. There is no mention whatsoever of razing the city to the ground. It is precisely that bearing in mind this objective Sarajevo was designated in the constitution of Republika Srpska as its capital. There was no mention of ever destroying Sarajevo. Why would they otherwise designate it as their capital? Sarajevo was seen as Serbs -- by Serbs as a town which historically belongs to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Is there any mention in this document, the one of the 12th May, to the possibility of razing to the ground the city of Sarajevo at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would like us now to come back to the map, the infamous map that you yourself developed and presented here, the map of targets. You have been asked questions about the chronological relationship of that map with the document you've seen. My question is as follows: Could you give us an idea of the number of legitimate targets in the city of Sarajevo? Could you briefly tell us the number of brigades, the number of battalions, the number of companies, and so on and so forth, present there so that we have a clearer picture how your map would look like if you had had the time or the relevant information?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's beyond the scope, and it was an issue that should have more properly been addressed in direct examination when they first took the witness to this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is my recollection well when I have in mind the witness said that 1500 targets would be in the city, or is it an incorrect recollection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. That is quite correct. I wanted him to say this differently. But anyway, thank you for this intervention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding the map, witness, and regarding the chronological aspect, that is, the time aspect, I want to ask you the following: What could you tell us regarding not only the chronological aspect but also the mobility of weapons? This mobility, could it have had an impact on the targets, or would they have had to be static?

utterances.speaker: The first had to do with this item 5 and the purpose of this
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would be the impact?

utterances.speaker: The first had to do with this item 5 and the purpose of this
utterances.text: There are static targets. In terms of space, a static target means that brigades did not leave their areas of responsibility, and I have shown the areas of responsibility of various brigades on the big map shown here on the board and you could see from that map that the 1st Corps in Sarajevo had 10 to 15 brigades throughout the war with minor changes in the volume of brigades. The areas of responsibility of brigades were fixed throughout the war. It could therefore be said that the position of sections as military targets and battalions as military targets were relatively static categories. However, weapons, sniper positions, firing positions of mortars, firing positions of cannons changed, shifted, but only within that zone of responsibility. Therefore, it could certainly happen that within one and the same brigade one target appeared as a potential target in several places. For instance, a battalion firing group, when changing the position of its mortar, could have been recorded three or four times as a target, although objectively it remained one group. But by shifting positions, the number of potential targets within one brigade changed. You have also to bear in mind another fact: When considering the total number of military targets in Sarajevo, according to the doctrine of All People's Defence that was in force and applied to all the three warring parties, all trailer trucks, cisterns, engineering machines, construction machinery, all vehicles for special purposes had their own wartime assignment. In times of war, they were requisitioned. And I did not consider them as military targets at all. So one has to know it is a certainty that there were many more military targets in Sarajevo than I depicted on my map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, as you correctly indicated at the beginning of your question that your question was not about the chronology, the only thing I think that was raised in cross-examination that was raised was the chronology. So I let you go, and the witness's answer, and the mobility that could have been dealt with easily also in examination-in-chief has been now answered. It's not the way of doing it to go through the whole map again, as you more or less were about to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Mr. President, I would like to ask another three questions, and I'm going to finish very soon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One question of methodology: If you had found documents which would have been obviously contrary to what you described as conclusions in your report, documents which are certain and dated, would you have used them or reacted to them in your report or what?

utterances.speaker: The first had to do with this item 5 and the purpose of this
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Certainly. And there were a lot of such documents. In fact, the majority of documents from the documentation of the 1st Corps of the BH army were in contradiction with the main claims made in the documents of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I analysed both categories of documents, looking for things which in my experience and in my view and in my knowledge could be true. I did not ignore a single piece of evidence from the Prosecution whose tapes I listened to, and I didn't ignore a single fact they asserted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In fact, I have just one or two more questions. The last would have to do with protests, and this has to do with the claim of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we'll deal with it very soon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of the elements that you were able to examine, documents, sources, primary or secondary, was there a contradiction - and if yes, what contradiction - between the fact that, as you said, from the beginning the Serb side wanted peace or strived for peace, specifically non-use of heavy weapons, and what is alleged in item 5 recently under examination? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. This does not arise out of cross-examination, Mr. President, and the issue of which side wanted peace was thoroughly covered in the direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Mr. President. This does arise because it's not only the claim of the Prosecution who dealt with this matter at length but since a certain number of questions were put by the Trial Chamber, I think that I am in a position to ask this witness to confirm what the attitude was of General Galic. This is what interests us, what the attitude was during the war with regard to the alleged claim that there was a desire to raze Sarajevo to the ground. And I think this is essential for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, in Mr. Piletta-Zanin's response he raises issues that may call for the witness to speculate and also a lack of foundation as to the accused's knowledge or state of mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. Please put your last question to the witness, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, General, following an intervention from the Prosecution you said that you hadn't found any documents that might show -- anything that might contradict your conclusions. My question is as follows: With regard to the documents about which the Prosecution asked you, were there any protests lodged by UNPROFOR, and if so what sort of protests and how were they processed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. That mischaracterises the nature of the cross-examination and the question which I put to the witness. The question wasn't whether he found any documents but what use he made of any such documents in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was also a question of methodology and not a question to enter into the area of -- you're going to the subject of the matter rather than to the methodology. If you'd have one final question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll confer, but I think that the response will be negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one last question. Ms. Pilipovic has asked for one last question. It concerns the methodology and perhaps the Trial Chamber. We have a tape we would like to have viewed. The witness on several occasions made reference to it. I don't know whether it would be a matter of interest for this Trial Chamber to view this cassette to see the elevated points around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Questions have been put in respect of elevated points. The witness has -- first of all, there's something played on the screen at this moment without my permission, so I would like that nothing would be played on the video evidence channel at this very moment. The matter has been raised in examination-in-chief. The Defence has chosen to do that without playing the tape. So therefore, it's not something that arises from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think that the day before yesterday a reference was made to the 4th JNA Corps and it was said that it was renamed as the new SRK. You said that they were not the same thing, that they were different troops, different corps. My question is: How were the relations, if any - if any - between the JNA and the VRS or the SRK in this case after the withdrawal of the JNA from Sarajevo in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: The first had to do with this item 5 and the purpose of this
utterances.text: At the time that was already the Army of Yugoslavia. It had been renamed as the Army of Yugoslavia. And after the withdrawal from Bosnia and Herzegovina, not a single regular unit of the Army of Yugoslavia participated in the combat on the side of the SRK. Unfortunately, at the time in Sarajevo other parts of the school centre, Marsal Tito, these were cadets and they had been withdrawn. That only succeeded in the month of June. They remained there, but this was not a combat section and they didn't participate in the fighting. And furthermore, the general staff and the Supreme Command of the Army of Yugoslavia certainly didn't have any direct or indirect influence on the command in the Republika Srpska, apart from the fact that attempts were made to achieve peace. This was in the framework of the Geneva negotiations and the contact established between delegations. The Yugoslav People's Army had influence on the Army of Republika Srpska in the sense that it assisted in taking care of the families of officers and non-commissioned officers who were members of the JNA and who had remained in the Army of Republika Srpska. They would receive salaries because the families would live from these salaries. They didn't have anything else to live off. And furthermore, they were provided with medical treatment in medical centres of the Army of Yugoslavia. The Army of Yugoslavia and Yugoslavia behaved as if it were a friendly country towards the Army of Republika Srpska and towards Republika Srpska, which was the political entity of the Serbian people. They behaved as a friend, not as allies, because being an ally involves a lot more than friendship does. And naturally it's a tradition -- there's a volunteer tradition among the Serbs and there were volunteers from all over the place. In all the wars that were waged by Serbs, there were volunteers. In the Second World War, 10.000 Serb volunteers came to fight for the liberation of Serbia, they came from America.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: In the First World War.

utterances.speaker: The first had to do with this item 5 and the purpose of this
utterances.text: I didn't manage to find a single document, a single indication, single decision that would show that there was any kind of direct influence of the Army of Yugoslavia on the Army of Republika Srpska after the withdrawal had taken place. In fact, this army was almost thrown out. They were left to the mercy of all those who wanted to disturb them, to interfere with them, because it's impossible for such an army to withdraw in 15 days in this manner from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday when you were referring to the relations between the SRK, between the commander and the officers of the SRK, you said that the commander was very well regarded by his subordinates. I would like you to have a look again on document D59 -- sorry, D259, the first paragraph. Could you read that paragraph aloud.

utterances.speaker: The first had to do with this item 5 and the purpose of this
utterances.text: Yes. "In spite of several orders and warnings issued by SRK commanders to the effect that fire shouldn't be opened on the city of Sarajevo from weapons of a large calibre, they are continuing to do so. Certain commanders, especially those of battalions and divisions, wilfully violate this order from the SRK commander and fail to take into account the consequences."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Does this paragraph show the consideration and obedience from battalion and division commanders to his chief, as you mentioned yesterday?

utterances.speaker: The first had to do with this item 5 and the purpose of this
utterances.text: This says that certain commanders did not respect this. It doesn't say that the entire commander system was not functioning. I said that Galic, the corps commander, did have certain problems with certain commanders, with the commander of the Igman Brigade, to an extent with the commander of the Ilijas Brigade, with certain paramilitary formations, and this shows that it was correct for the corps commander to repeat in his orders that fire should not be opened on the city without his authorisation or the authorisation of the operative centre or the system of command according to his decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were referring to your handwritten notes and you made -- well, reference were made to snipers, ask you said, answering a question of the Prosecutor, that sniper squads were established in the second half of 1994. Do you recall it?

utterances.speaker: The first had to do with this item 5 and the purpose of this
utterances.text: Yes, sniper groups, sniper units. People called them in various ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Could you elaborate a little bit on that. That is, when, where, how were those squads established and whether they were established more or less at the same time by the SRK and the BiH army or not, something about that.

utterances.speaker: The first had to do with this item 5 and the purpose of this
utterances.text: In the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, sniper units existed a lot earlier. I mentioned a number of documents which show that the battalions had sniper units and the brigades had sniper platoons, but the 1st Corps as early as 1993 set aside snipers and formed sniper units at the level of a corps, and this was to be -- these were to be units that would be under the command of the 1st Corps commander. The Sarajevo Romanija Corps didn't do this and it didn't have sniper units during the relevant period of time that I analysed, during General Galic's mandate. I didn't come across any documents showing that sniper units had been formed as part of the corps or as part of his -- of its subordinate units. And afterwards -- after that I didn't analyse any document, documents that concern the period when General Galic no longer had the mandate. But commanders told me that in the second half of 1994 they formed sniper groups as anti-sniping units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: General Radinovic, unfortunately we are not able to finish today because it's quarter to 2.00 and Judge El Mahdi would have questions for you, I might have some questions for you as well. So I'll give you the same instruction as I did the last few days, that you should not speak about your testimony given or still to be given in this court. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As there are a few translation issues, could someone from the French booth come to see me. I would be very grateful if they could show me such kindness. Thank you. After the hearing, so that we don't waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd prefer to have it -- how much time would it take to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can do it very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there was a problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not much time at all. It has to do with yesterday, above all. There was a problem. The witness never said what we can see in the French transcript. He never said that he had a request to make to the general. That might imply something. He spoke about a general request. And on page 7 we have "before" instead of "afterwards"; page 16, we're not talking about a person who was accused but a person accused -- not the accused but an accused; and on line 21, it's a matter of spelling that should be verified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Before I adjourn, General Galic, when I am well informed today is your 60th birthday. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, today is my 60th birthday. My 61st year is about to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although the Chamber is fully aware that the circumstances are not such that you would wish at your birthday, we nevertheless would like to congratulate you with your birthday and wish you at least a pleasant remainder of the day, and we hope that you still can enjoy at least a bit your birthday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours, I'd like to thank you and everyone else here. Everyone has to bear their cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00.
